paragraphs: Estimating an object's orientation from a single image requires a model to represent three-dimensional rotations. Common representations, including Euler angles and quaternions, can introduce discontinuities or singularities. They also fit awkwardly with spherical convolutional networks, whose calculations take place in a frequency representation. The paper addresses this mismatch between how a network processes information and how it is asked to express an orientation.

The proposed predictor directly outputs Wigner-D coefficients, a frequency-domain representation of rotations. Its training loss also compares predictions in that domain. This keeps the prediction target aligned with the network's internal operations. The architecture is SO(3)-equivariant, meaning its predictions transform consistently when rotations are applied, giving the method a structured way to handle changes in orientation.

The authors report state-of-the-art results on ModelNet10-SO(3) and PASCAL3D+, with improvements in accuracy, robustness, and data efficiency. These findings support matching the rotation representation to an equivariant network's computational structure, rather than treating the output representation as an independent design choice.
neurips-2024-3d-equivariant-pose-regress.tldr: Predicting rotations directly as Wigner-D coefficients aligns pose estimation with spherical networks and improves reported accuracy, robustness, and data efficiency.

paragraphs: Autoregressive language models generate text through repeated sampling steps, making generation a major inference bottleneck. Speculative decoding accelerates this process by asking a smaller model to propose several tokens and a larger model to validate them. Although this approach has demonstrated practical benefits, the paper argues that its theoretical explanation has lagged behind its empirical use.

The authors represent decoding through a Markov-chain abstraction and study both output quality and computational acceleration within that framework. Their analysis considers theoretical limits, batch algorithms, and tradeoffs between quality and speed. This puts several aspects of speculative decoding into a common mathematical setting, allowing their relationships to be examined together.

A central finding connects different model components through total variation distances, which describe differences between probability distributions. The analysis shows how these relationships jointly affect decoding efficiency. Its contribution is therefore an explanation of the factors governing speculative decoding, including how quality requirements interact with acceleration, rather than a claim that one speedup applies across all model combinations.
neurips-2024-a-theoretical-perspective-f.tldr: A Markov-chain analysis explains speculative decoding's theoretical limits and how differences between model distributions affect speed and output quality.

paragraphs: Simulation-based inference works backward from observations to plausible parameters of a stochastic simulator. Neural posterior estimation learns a probability distribution over those parameters, but collecting enough simulations can be expensive. This becomes particularly difficult when the parameter space is large and each simulator run consumes substantial resources.

Active sequential neural posterior estimation, or ASNPE, introduces active learning into that process. It estimates how useful candidate simulation parameters would be to the probabilistic model and uses that assessment to guide further sampling. The acquisition scheme can be incorporated into existing posterior-estimation pipelines with low computational overhead. Its purpose is to make the simulation budget more informative, improving sample efficiency.

The authors demonstrate the method on travel-demand calibration for a large real-world traffic network, a high-dimensional problem involving expensive traffic simulation. ASNPE outperforms well-tuned benchmarks and state-of-the-art posterior estimators there. It also improves over non-active counterparts across simulation-based inference benchmarks, supporting active selection as a practical way to improve how posterior estimators use simulation samples.
neurips-2024-active-sequential-posterior.tldr: ASNPE actively selects informative simulation parameters to improve posterior estimation's sample efficiency with low additional computational overhead.

paragraphs: Graph convolutions combine information across a graph to help classify its nodes. Repeating them can initially help, but excessive repetition may make node representations too similar, a problem called oversmoothing. This paper studies a corrected convolution that removes the principal eigenvector contribution, examining whether useful information can continue to accumulate without the usual deterioration.

The theoretical analysis uses a two-class contextual stochastic block model, a specified probabilistic setting for graph structure and node features. For partial classification, the authors show that successive corrected convolutions can reduce misclassification error exponentially until a saturation level is reached. Beyond that level, performance does not worsen within the analyzed setting. They also extend the analysis to multiple classes with Gaussian-mixture features.

For exact classification, the separability threshold can improve exponentially for up to O(log n / log log n) corrected convolutions. Together, these results distinguish saturation from degradation: additional processing may stop helping without becoming harmful. The guarantees are tied to the paper's graph and feature models, providing a rigorous explanation under those assumptions.
neurips-2024-analysis-of-corrected-graph.tldr: Under specified random-graph models, removing the principal eigenvector allows repeated graph convolutions to improve classification until saturation without oversmoothing-related degradation.

paragraphs: Dataset condensation creates a small synthetic training set intended to preserve the usefulness of a full dataset. Much existing work focuses on classification, where two models can agree on a predicted label even if their underlying output scores differ. Time-series forecasting demands closer agreement: predicted numerical values must remain similar across the forecast, making successful condensation more demanding.

The authors analyze the condensation objective for forecasting and derive CondTSF, a small plugin for existing condensation methods. Its purpose is to reduce the distance between forecasts from a model trained on synthetic data and those from a model trained on the full dataset. This directly addresses the kind of agreement that matters for forecasting rather than relying only on criteria suited to classification.

Across eight time-series datasets, CondTSF improves every previously developed condensation method evaluated in the study. The gains are especially pronounced at low condensation ratios, where very little synthetic data is retained. The findings support adapting condensation objectives to numerical prediction when seeking lower storage and training costs.
neurips-2024-condtsf-one-line-plugin-of-.tldr: CondTSF improves time-series dataset condensation by encouraging synthetic-data-trained models to match the numerical forecasts of full-data-trained models.

paragraphs: Predictive models face a moving target when the distribution of their data changes over time. Temporal domain generalization studies this problem, but approaches built around fixed time intervals can miss dynamics in continuously changing systems observed at irregular times. This paper formalizes continuous temporal domain generalization, allowing domain observations to arrive at arbitrary times.

The proposed Koodos framework describes the problem as a continuous dynamical system and uses Koopman theory to learn its underlying evolution. It addresses the dynamics of both the data and the models, including complex nonlinear changes in high-dimensional settings. An accompanying optimization strategy uses prior knowledge about patterns in those dynamics to support analysis and control of generalization.

The authors report extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution combines a problem formulation with a method for handling it: observation times become part of a continuously evolving process rather than merely a sequence of discrete domains. This matters for learning from irregular temporal data while explicitly accounting for how predictive conditions change.
neurips-2024-continuous-temporal-domain-.tldr: Koodos uses a continuous dynamical-system formulation and Koopman theory to generalize across changing data distributions observed at irregular times.

paragraphs: Estimating depth from a single panoramic image is difficult because 360-degree imagery uses different projections and distortions from ordinary perspective images. Models trained for perspective views therefore do not transfer directly. Depth Anywhere addresses this mismatch by using strong perspective-depth models to help train panoramic depth estimators with unlabeled 360-degree data.

The framework projects a panorama onto six cube faces, giving the teacher models perspective views from which to generate depth pseudo-labels. These generated labels provide training information for otherwise unlabeled panoramas. The pipeline includes offline masking of invalid regions and an online semi-supervised training stage, combining these components into a way to transfer depth knowledge across camera projections.

Experiments on Matterport3D and Stanford2D3D show significant accuracy improvements, particularly in zero-shot scenarios. The authors present the pipeline as applicable to any monocular 360-degree depth estimator. The results support using existing perspective models and growing unlabeled panoramic collections together, making cross-projection knowledge transfer a central part of improving panoramic depth estimation.
neurips-2024-depth-anywhere-enhancing-36.tldr: Depth Anywhere transfers perspective-depth knowledge to 360-degree estimators through cube-face pseudo-labels and semi-supervised training on unlabeled panoramas.

paragraphs: Convolutional image networks exploit a natural symmetry: shifting an image should shift its processed representation consistently. General graphs lack an equivalent notion of spatial translation. This paper instead studies graph functional shifts, defined as unitary transformations that commute with the graph shift operator. These symmetries transform signals on a graph rather than directly moving positions in space.

Standard spectral graph networks respect these transformations in their linear filtering layers, but ordinary activation functions break the symmetry. The authors propose nonlinear spectral filters that preserve it throughout the nonlinear operation. Their construction uses a new spectral-domain representation designed to transfer between graphs, addressing both symmetry preservation and the portability of spectral processing.

The paper establishes universal approximation properties for the proposed filters and reports better node- and graph-classification performance than existing spectral graph networks. The theoretical and empirical contributions serve different roles: one characterizes expressive capability, while the other demonstrates usefulness on benchmarks. Together, they support building nonlinear graph models around a precisely defined signal-space symmetry.
neurips-2024-equivariant-machine-learnin.tldr: Nonlinear spectral filters preserve graph functional-shift symmetry while providing universal approximation properties and improved reported classification performance.

paragraphs: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and dynamic range, making them useful for reconstruction under fast motion and low light. Existing event-based approaches commonly use neural radiance fields, but these can require time-consuming training and inference and offer limited scene editing. Event-3DGS introduces Gaussian splatting as a representation for reconstructing scenes directly from event streams and synthesizing new viewpoints.

The framework jointly optimizes scene and sensor parameters, treating the reconstruction and the event-producing sensor together. It adds a photovoltage estimation module based on a high-pass filter to reduce event noise. An event-specific reconstruction loss supplies the objective used to optimize the method for reconstruction quality.

The authors report better reconstruction quality than state-of-the-art methods on simulated and real-world datasets. They also demonstrate robust reconstruction in tested real-world conditions involving extreme noise, fast movement, and low illumination. These findings support the combination of a Gaussian scene representation and explicit event-data modeling for demanding capture conditions, including cases where event noise complicates reconstruction.
neurips-2024-event-3dgs-event-based-3d-r.tldr: Event-3DGS reconstructs scenes from event streams using Gaussian splatting, joint scene-sensor optimization, and noise-aware event modeling.

paragraphs: Learning from synchronized images and LiDAR point clouds can transfer visual knowledge into three-dimensional representations. Contrastive training, however, can create a conflict: unmatched pixels and points may be pushed apart even when they describe the same semantic class. This separates features that should share meaning and can undermine the learned representation.

The proposed method uses off-the-shelf visual foundation models to generate semantic pixel labels for weakly supervised pixel-to-point distillation. It also organizes the feature space using von Mises-Fisher distributions so that embeddings from the same class remain consistent across inputs. These components bring semantic information into both the training supervision and the organization of learned features.

A further sampling adjustment accounts for uneven spatial distributions and category frequencies among points, supporting more balanced learning. Experiments show that the combined approach mitigates the conflicts found in traditional methods and consistently outperforms existing image-to-LiDAR contrastive distillation methods on downstream tasks. The findings emphasize that useful cross-modal matching requires attention to shared meaning as well as individual pixel-point correspondences.
neurips-2024-fine-grained-image-to-lidar.tldr: Semantic labels, class-consistent feature distributions, and balanced point sampling improve image-to-LiDAR distillation by reducing conflicting contrastive signals.

paragraphs: Generating audio for a silent video requires sounds that match both its content and the timing of visible events. Frieren tackles audio quality, synchronization, and generation efficiency together using rectified flow matching. It learns a video-conditioned vector field that transports noise toward a latent representation of an audio spectrogram along straight paths.

Sampling follows this learned field by solving an ordinary differential equation. A feed-forward Transformer estimates the field without generating the audio autoregressively, while channel-level fusion of visual and audio features supports temporal alignment. Reflow and guided one-step distillation further allow the model to produce decent audio with only a few sampling steps, or even one.

On VGGSound, the authors report state-of-the-art generation quality and temporal alignment, including 97.22% alignment accuracy and a 6.2% inception-score improvement over a strong diffusion baseline. The abstract also reports quality advantages over autoregressive and score-based models. The reduced-step result is described as producing decent audio, so it should be distinguished from a claim that every sampling configuration achieves the headline benchmark performance.
neurips-2024-frieren-efficient-video-to-.tldr: Frieren uses rectified flow matching and temporally aligned feature fusion to generate synchronized video audio, with distillation enabling few-step or one-step sampling.

paragraphs: Complex image requests can require several capabilities that a single generation or editing model does not possess. Existing systems also struggle with intricate prompts and often lack ways to verify and correct their outputs. GenArtist addresses these problems by placing a multimodal language-model agent in charge of a library of existing image tools.

The agent breaks a complex request into simpler subproblems and organizes generation, editing, and correction into a tree-structured plan. It selects and executes tools while verifying results step by step. When a tool needs position-related inputs that the request does not provide, the system generates those inputs and incorporates spatial information into the operation.

Experiments show that GenArtist handles varied generation and editing tasks, with reported state-of-the-art performance exceeding models including SDXL and DALL-E 3. The contribution is a coordinated workflow in which planning, spatial input preparation, and self-correction connect specialized models. The findings support treating complex image creation as a sequence of checked operations rather than relying entirely on one model's capabilities.
neurips-2024-genartist-multimodal-llm-as.tldr: GenArtist coordinates specialized image tools through a multimodal agent that plans, verifies, and corrects complex generation and editing workflows.

paragraphs: Graph autoencoders learn representations by compressing graph information and reconstructing it. HC-GAE builds this process around hierarchical clusters so that the representation captures structural patterns at multiple levels. During encoding, hard node assignments divide the graph into separate subgraphs, each of which is compressed into a node in a smaller, coarsened graph.

During decoding, soft assignments expand the coarsened nodes to reconstruct the original structure. The hierarchical compression and expansion provide structural features in both directions. A redesigned loss incorporates information from either the encoder or decoder, allowing the learning objective to use information generated across the reconstruction process.

Graph convolution is restricted to individual separated subgraphs, preventing that operation from propagating node information between them. The authors argue that this significantly reduces oversmoothing, where repeated convolution makes representations overly similar. Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate effective representations for both node and graph classification. The approach therefore combines multilevel structural learning with a restriction on information mixing intended to preserve distinctions within the learned representations.
neurips-2024-hc-gae-the-hierarchical-clu.tldr: HC-GAE learns hierarchical graph representations through cluster compression and reconstruction while restricting convolution to reduce oversmoothing.

paragraphs: Multimodal learning often seeks information shared across different feature spaces while separating it from modality-specific variation. Earlier identifiability results show that shared components can be recovered from linear mixtures when corresponding samples are paired. This paper asks when recovery remains possible without knowing which observations across modalities belong together.

The authors propose a loss that minimizes divergence between distributions and derive sufficient conditions for identifying the shared components. These conditions characterize cross-modality distribution differences and rule out density-preserving transformations that would create ambiguity. The conditions are described as milder than those in existing approaches based on independent component analysis, broadening the theoretical settings in which unpaired recovery can be justified.

Additional structural constraints, motivated by available side information, allow further relaxation of the conditions. Synthetic and real-world experiments validate the identifiability claims. The result establishes circumstances in which pairing is unnecessary for recovery under a linear-mixture model; it does not claim that distribution matching uniquely identifies shared information for arbitrary unpaired multimodal data.
neurips-2024-identifiable-shared-compone.tldr: The paper derives sufficient conditions for recovering shared components from unpaired multimodal linear mixtures through distribution-divergence minimization.

paragraphs: Training new neural networks becomes increasingly resource-intensive as models grow. Model LEGO explores reusing parts of trained convolutional classifiers to construct models for specific tasks without training the newly assembled model. Its Model Disassembling and Assembling framework treats useful task-related components as building blocks that can be located, extracted, and recombined.

During disassembly, a notion of relative contribution helps identify components relevant to a task. During assembly, alignment padding and parameter scaling make those extracted components usable together in a new model. The approach is inspired by information pathways in biological vision, but its practical focus is on finding and combining task-aware computation already present in trained CNNs.

Experiments show that extracted components and assembled models can closely match or surpass the baseline's performance. The authors also explore decision-route analysis, compression, and knowledge distillation as applications. These results support component-level model reuse as a promising alternative source of task-specific models, with the reported evidence centered on components obtained from trained convolutional classifiers.
neurips-2024-model-lego-creating-models-.tldr: Model LEGO extracts task-aware components from trained CNNs and recombines them into new models without additional training.

paragraphs: Generating music from motion and generating motion from music have largely been studied as separate tasks. MoMu-Diffusion brings them into a shared framework aimed at producing long sequences whose motion and music remain synchronized. The central challenge is to model correspondence between the two modalities while managing the computational cost of lengthy inputs.

A bidirectional contrastive rhythmic variational autoencoder first extracts compact, aligned representations of motion and music. Working in these latent spaces reduces the computational burden associated with long sequences. A multimodal diffusion Transformer then uses the aligned representations, together with cross-guidance sampling, to support cross-modal generation, multimodal generation, and outputs of different lengths.

The authors report qualitative and quantitative improvements over recent state-of-the-art methods. Generated sequences are described as realistic, diverse, long-term, and matched to the beat. These findings support learning motion and music correspondence jointly: the shared representation provides a foundation for several generation tasks while keeping rhythmic alignment central to the model's handling of the two modalities.
neurips-2024-momu-diffusion-on-learning-.tldr: MoMu-Diffusion combines aligned motion-music latent representations with diffusion generation to produce long, diverse, beat-synchronized sequences.

paragraphs: Inverse rendering attempts to recover geometry, materials, and illumination separately from images. Reflective objects complicate this separation because their appearance includes light reflected from other surfaces. Methods that neglect indirect illumination can therefore struggle with scenes containing several smooth objects whose reflections interact.

Ref-MC2 uses repeated Monte Carlo sampling to account for both environmental illumination and light reflected from object surfaces. Because additional sampling increases computation, a specularity-adaptive strategy reduces the computational burden. The method also addresses geometry: errors can accumulate across repeated reflections, so a reflection-aware surface model initializes the geometry and refines it during inverse rendering.

The authors introduce a challenging dataset of multiple objects with inter-reflections and report better results than other inverse-rendering methods across various object groups. Relighting and material-editing demonstrations illustrate the recovered separation of scene properties. The work connects illumination modeling, sampling efficiency, and geometric accuracy, showing why all three matter when reconstructing scenes in which objects visibly reflect one another.
neurips-2024-multi-times-monte-carlo-ren.tldr: Ref-MC2 reconstructs mutually reflective objects using repeated light sampling, specularity-adaptive computation, and reflection-aware geometry refinement.

paragraphs: A neural network trained on a sequence of tasks can become increasingly difficult to train on new ones. The paper groups this concern under issues such as plasticity loss, trainability loss, and primacy bias. In continual reinforcement learning, preserving the ability to keep learning is therefore an important objective alongside performance on the tasks already encountered.

The proposed intervention is Parseval regularization, which maintains orthogonality in the network's weight matrices. The intended role is to preserve useful optimization properties as training continues. This makes the structure of the learned weights a direct target of regularization, connecting the network's internal organization to its ability to adapt during a sequence of reinforcement-learning tasks.

The authors report significant benefits for agents across gridworld, CARL, and MetaWorld tasks. They also conduct ablations to investigate the source of those benefits and examine weight-matrix rank, weight norms, and policy entropy as trainability-related measurements. The findings support orthogonality regularization as a useful intervention in the tested continual-learning settings, while the accompanying analyses examine how network properties relate to continued learning.
neurips-2024-parseval-regularization-for.tldr: Parseval regularization maintains orthogonal weight matrices to help reinforcement-learning agents retain their ability to learn across successive tasks.

paragraphs: Adversarial prompts can cause aligned language models to produce harmful outputs despite their intended safeguards. Earlier attacks commonly assumed access to model weights or relied on transferability, where a prompt developed against one model also works against another. This paper examines an attacker who can query a remote model through its API.

The proposed query-based approach uses that access to construct adversarial examples for the remote target. The authors report that these examples produce harmful strings with substantially higher probability than transfer-only attacks. The distinction matters because API interaction supplies information from the target itself, creating a different evaluation setting from attacks that depend only on success elsewhere.

The study validates the attack on GPT-3.5 and OpenAI's safety classifier. It reports harmful GPT-3.5 outputs that existing transfer attacks failed to elicit, along with nearly 100% evasion probability for the evaluated OpenAI and Llama Guard classifiers. These are findings about the tested systems and attack setting. They show that assessments based on transfer attacks alone can understate the vulnerabilities exposed by query-based adversarial testing.
neurips-2024-query-based-adversarial-pro.tldr: Query-based adversarial testing finds substantially stronger attacks than transfer-only methods against the evaluated language model and safety classifiers.

paragraphs: Interactive segmentation lets users guide an image's segmentation through inputs such as clicks. Many benchmarks assume that users click at the center of the largest incorrectly segmented area. Actual users do not always follow that rule, so a method's benchmark score may give an overly favorable impression of its performance in practical use.

The authors collected 475,000 real-user clicks through a large crowdsourcing study. They used those observations, together with ideas from saliency research, to build a clickability model that samples clicks resembling human inputs. RClicks combines this model and dataset into a benchmark that examines both average segmentation quality and robustness to different clicking patterns.

The benchmark indicates that interactive segmentation models may perform worse with realistic clicks than conventional evaluations suggest, and that most evaluated methods lack robustness to click patterns. The contribution is therefore also about evaluation design: user behavior becomes an explicit part of measuring a system's usefulness. Better performance under one idealized clicking strategy does not necessarily imply a better experience across the ways people actually interact.
neurips-2024-rclicks-realistic-click-sim.tldr: RClicks uses 475,000 human clicks to benchmark interactive segmentation under realistic behavior, revealing performance and robustness gaps.

paragraphs: Mobile-health systems can use contextual bandits to choose interventions suited to a person's current circumstances. Learning those choices is difficult when participants differ, responses change over time, and reward relationships are nonlinear. RoME addresses these challenges through a mixed-effects model that distinguishes the differential reward associated with interventions from the potentially complex baseline reward.

The algorithm uses user-specific and time-specific random effects to represent variation in differential rewards. It combines these with network cohesion penalties and debiased machine learning for flexible baseline-reward estimation. This division allows the method to account for a complicated background response while separately modeling the reward differences that guide intervention choices.

The authors establish a high-probability regret bound whose dimensional dependence comes solely from the differential-reward model, allowing robust bounds even with a highly complex baseline. They also report superior performance in a simulation and two off-policy evaluation studies. The results connect a theoretical benefit of separating reward components with empirical evidence from evaluations of intervention-selection performance.
neurips-2024-rome-a-robust-mixed-effects.tldr: RoME combines mixed effects and flexible baseline estimation to personalize mobile-health interventions while controlling regret through the differential-reward model.

paragraphs: Shared autonomy combines a human's control inputs with an AI copilot's assistance. A constantly active copilot can restrict the person's autonomy, even though the amount of useful assistance changes with the situation. This paper proposes selective intervention: the copilot acts only when its action has a higher expected value than the human's proposed action.

The resulting system, IDA, implements this rule with a diffusion copilot trained on expert demonstrations using goal masking. Its assistance is goal-agnostic. The paper proves a lower bound on IDA's performance relative to human performance in its formal treatment, providing theoretical support for intervention that helps without reducing the human's control performance.

With simulated pilots, IDA outperforms both unassisted control and traditional shared autonomy in Reacher variants and Lunar Lander. Human-in-the-loop Lunar Lander experiments also show improved control, greater experienced autonomy, and participant preference for IDA. The authors attribute these results to preserving human decision-making while intervening to prevent universally bad states, connecting selective assistance with both task performance and the user's experience of control.
neurips-2024-shared-autonomy-with-ida-in.tldr: IDA selectively intervenes when a diffusion copilot's action has higher expected value, improving reported control performance and perceived human autonomy.

paragraphs: Federated learning must sometimes coordinate devices with very different model capacities and dataset sizes. Knowledge distillation can share their knowledge, but merging all teacher outputs can dilute informative signals from stronger devices. Giving every student the same merged target also overlooks differences in what each student can learn and what each device contributes.

TAKFL treats knowledge transfer from each device prototype's ensemble as a separate task. It distills those tasks independently, preserving their distinct contributions, and uses distillation-based self-regularization to mitigate noise in the unsupervised ensemble-distillation process. An adaptive task-arithmetic step then combines the separately distilled knowledge in a way customized to each student model.

The paper provides theoretical results supporting task arithmetic for knowledge transfer across devices of varying capacities. Evaluations on computer-vision and natural-language-processing tasks report state-of-the-art results and significant improvements over existing distillation-based methods. The contribution is a separation between acquiring knowledge from different sources and deciding how a particular student should integrate it, making device diversity central to the transfer process.
neurips-2024-towards-diverse-device-hete.tldr: TAKFL separately distills knowledge from different device prototypes and adaptively combines it for each student's learning capacity.

paragraphs: Standard mesh texturing maps a three-dimensional surface into a two-dimensional UV layout. That process can introduce seams, distortion, duplicated vertices, wasted space, and uneven surface resolution, particularly with automatic unwrapping. This paper instead represents a texture as colored points on the object's surface, avoiding the need to generate it in a UV plane.

A denoising diffusion probabilistic model generates the point colors while remaining constrained to the surface. Heat diffusion across the mesh allows spatial communication between points. This makes the object's surface geometry part of how texture information is exchanged, supporting a model designed to accommodate different point samplings and resolutions.

The authors introduce fast resampling of the mesh's spectral properties so heat diffusion can process arbitrarily sampled point-cloud textures. They also introduce heat-diffusion-based self-attention to support consistency over long distances. The contribution is a surface-based generation framework that connects flexible texture sampling with geometric communication, addressing the representation and coordination problems that arise when replacing a fixed two-dimensional texture layout.
neurips-2024-uv-free-texture-generation-.tldr: The method generates textures directly as colored surface points, using heat diffusion and surface-aware attention instead of UV layouts.

paragraphs: Personalized retrieval and segmentation aim to find a particular instance from a reference image and short description. Recognizing the right category is insufficient when several instances of that category are present. The paper identifies this distinction as a weakness of self-supervised foundation models, even when their overall results are comparable to supervised approaches.

Personalized Diffusion Features Matching, or PDM, uses intermediate features from pretrained text-to-image diffusion models to perform these personalization tasks. It requires no additional training. The approach examines whether representations already learned by a generative model can distinguish the requested instance well enough to support both finding relevant images and locating the instance within them.

PDM outperforms methods on popular retrieval and segmentation benchmarks, including supervised approaches. The authors also identify shortcomings in existing instance and segmentation datasets and propose new benchmarks. These contributions address both representation choice and evaluation: strong personalization requires measuring whether a system finds the particular reference instance, especially when category-level recognition alone cannot resolve the task.
neurips-2024-where-s-waldo-diffusion-fea.tldr: PDM uses pretrained diffusion-model features without additional training to improve retrieval and segmentation of specific instances.
